title: The Virtualizor Attack: An Unmitigated Threat Affecting Millions of Websites
summary: The Virtualizor supply-chain compromise shows how a BGP hijack can defeat TLS, bypass RPKI and multi-perspective validation, and expose millions of websites through permissive route configurations.
body_markdown:
The cloud management software company Virtualizor was recently hit by a major infrastructure attack that let the adversary distribute malicious software packages to customers. The attack involved a malicious routing update that was used to obtain a valid TLS certificate. With the TLS certificate, the adversary was able to terminate the victim's HTTPS connections while impersonating the victim. For me, this type of attack is personal. I wrote the first academic paper to study this attack type back in 2018 (at the time, there were no known instances of this attack). Since then, I have spent a significant portion of my career trying to mitigate attacks like these, including creating a standard that now protects the issuance of every HTTPS certificate and starting a company. Sadly, a large portion of the Internet remains vulnerable, and the potential for these attacks to cause massive damage is still there.


## The attack itself


On August 28, 2026, a block of IP addresses belonging to the hosting provider Hetzner was maliciously announced in the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP, the backbone routing protocol of the Internet), likely by NexonHost (AS62390). The cause could have been a compromise at NexonHost, intentional malicious behavior, or someone else using its ASN maliciously. It is hard to say for sure, but the external effect of the hijack is clear: Internet traffic that should have been going to Hetzner was redirected to NexonHost.


BGP hijacks (or varying types of mishaps) are sadly somewhat common due to the inherent lack of authentication in the routing protocol, which was developed back in the 1990s. I think those who work with BGP often consider it a leaky bucket. BGP security regularly rises to the level of government concern about infrastructure security, as reflected in[Ars Technica's coverage of this attack](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/09/well-executed-bgp-attack-uses-hijacked-ips-to-infect-real-networks/) . That said, there is a silver lining: encryption. BGP hijacks reroute plaintext traffic, so if traffic is end-to-end encrypted with TLS, it should be fine, right? The adversary would just see the encrypted bytes. Sadly, this is not the way web TLS works.


## “Bamboozling” TLS with the BGP hijack


Trusted digital certificates that vouch for the identity of domain names like` google.com` are signed using plaintext connections. TLS connections rely on digital certificates to authenticate the server at the other end of the encrypted tunnel. Digital certificates contain a domain name like` google.com` and the cryptographic key that will be used by the Google server at the other end. If someone else can get a digital certificate with their public key and the domain name` google.com` , they can impersonate a` google.com` server in TLS connections and read the encrypted data that was supposed to be sent to Google. To prevent digital certificates from being forged, they are signed by a small number of trusted Certificate Authorities (CAs).


Sadly, the process by which digital certificates are signed is based on plaintext data. When someone requests a certificate from a CA, the CA needs to verify that the person actually controls the domains contained in the certificate. This process, known as domain control validation, can include putting a piece of plaintext in DNS or at the web server of the requested domain. If an adversary can trick this plaintext connection (for example, via a BGP hijack), the adversary can get a certificate for a domain it does not control. With this certificate, the adversary can impersonate the victim's website, decrypt data intended for the victim, and serve malicious responses such as corrupted software updates. In 2018, I wrote the first scientific paper on this attack,[Bamboozling Certificate Authorities with BGP](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity18/presentation/birge-lee) . This is exactly what happened in the Virtualizor attack.


## What can (and has) been done to stop this?


This attack spans many layers of the network stack and involves many technologies. At each layer, initiatives exist to stop these attacks or at least make them more difficult. One such initiative at the TLS layer that is deployed universally on all certificate issuance is MPIC, which I personally spearheaded. Sadly, even with these technologies, the percentage of top web domains that could be affected by an attack like this is likely in the mid-double digits.


### At the BGP layer


A natural response is to trace the attack back to its root cause and conclude that BGP routing should be locked down. After all, BGP is the core routing protocol of the Internet. From a defense-in-depth perspective, allowing adversaries to intercept arbitrary network traffic is a large vulnerability, even when encrypted channels exist. The good news is that the U.S. government agrees with this stance, and the White House previously published a[major initiative to improve BGP security](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/06/sustaining-select-efforts-to-strengthen-the-nations-cybersecurity-and-amending-executive-order-13694-and-executive-order-14144/) . The bad news is that BGP is a distributed system with decentralized governance, so security technologies must function during partial adoption while networks around the globe upgrade. Thus, the problem is not as simple as making people deploy secure BGP. There is an upgraded variant of BGP called BGPSEC, but it sits at 0% deployment on the Internet backbone.


The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) has emerged as the main next step in BGP security. RPKI creates a cryptographic database of who operates which IP address blocks. Sadly, this is not a bulletproof solution, as RPKI does not stop a network from claiming to have a route to a victim's IP block. The good news is that when RPKI is in place (and configured correctly, as I will discuss in a moment), an adversary's attacks become highly localized, typically affecting less than 50% of the Internet. This localization occurs because the victim's route is one hop shorter than the adversary's route. NIST currently tracks RPKI as[protecting almost 70% of all routes](https://rpki-monitor.antd.nist.gov/) , and[many of the major carriers have adopted it](https://isbgpsafeyet.com/) .


### At the TLS layer


The primary technology at the TLS layer for mitigating the impact of BGP attacks is Multi-Perspective Issuance Corroboration (MPIC). I played a significant role in its creation, development, standardization, and implementation. I went from being the lead author of the paper that introduced MPIC to writing the normative standard for MPIC deployment that all CAs must follow and founding the open-source implementation that performs MPIC for over 30% of all HTTPS certificates.


MPIC involves CAs performing domain control validation from multiple perspectives spread across the Internet. The CA only signs a certificate if enough of the perspectives agree that domain control validation passed. This is often *n* −1, allowing one perspective to fail for operational robustness while still being as strict as possible. MPIC is designed to detect localized BGP attacks (i.e., equally specific BGP attacks) because it relies on some perspectives remaining unaffected by the adversary's attack to prevent certificate issuance.


## Where the gap still exists


There is a really nice synergy between MPIC and RPKI: RPKI forces attacks to be very localized, while MPIC detects localized attacks and ensures they do not lead to TLS certificates. With RPKI at 70%, including adoption by most large service providers, and MPIC at 100% thanks to a global CA/Browser Forum mandate, it seems like a large portion of this problem is solved. Sadly, that is not the case: the routes hijacked in the Virtualizor attack were protected with RPKI, and the CA that signed the malicious certificate, Let's Encrypt, had a strong MPIC deployment. So what happened?


Earlier, I said an RPKI-protected route is unlikely to be globally hijacked, but this was an oversimplification. To get to the root of this, I need to briefly explain longest-prefix-match routing. BGP routes cover blocks of IP addresses of varying sizes, often called IP prefixes, and routers always use the most specific route they know to reach a destination. This system is known as longest-prefix-match routing. Suppose you wanted to reach Los Angeles and saw one road sign for “California” and another for “Los Angeles.” You would take the road to Los Angeles. If there were no Los Angeles sign, you would probably fall back and first drive to California.


Routers do the same thing. If they are routing a packet with an IP address of` 1.2.3.4` and they hit a routing table with routes to` 1.2.*.*` and` 1.2.3.*` , they will prefer the route to` 1.2.3.*` because it is more specific. Sadly, this behavior can be exploited during a BGP hijack, as the adversary can get the entire Internet to prefer its route just by announcing a more specific IP prefix than the victim. These more-specific, or sub-prefix, BGP hijacks are typically global or near-global in their impact.


*Technical note: Hijacks of equally specific prefixes (for example, competing routes to` 1.2.*.*` ) are typically localized because the victim's and adversary's routes are to the same prefix. That brings a long list of route tie-breakers into play, including shortest path. Vantage points therefore tend to route to the victim or adversary based on which one is topologically closer, causing a split in the Internet rather than the wipeout effect of a sub-prefix hijack.*


RPKI prevents sub-prefix hijacks by allowing networks both to assert ownership of an IP block and to specify exactly which prefix lengths can be announced in BGP. An RPKI entry for` 1.2.*.*` , or` 1.2.0.0/16` in CIDR notation, can permit exactly` 1.2.0.0/16` to be announced in BGP. If an adversary tries to announce` 1.2.3.*` (` 1.2.3.0/24` ) and capture all traffic with a sub-prefix hijack, this route will be dropped by routers that are filtering RPKI correctly.


But like all good security standards, there is a loophole. RPKI also permits an authorization to specify something called a max length. The max length allows more-specific BGP announcements to be RPKI-valid. An RPKI object for` 1.2.0.0/16` with a max length of 24 permits BGP announcements for sub-prefixes of` 1.2.0.0/16` , including` 1.2.3.0/24` . Now, the adversary can announce its devastating, globally impactful sub-prefix hijack and still pass as RPKI-valid.


This max-length issue is what happened in the Virtualizor hijack. Virtualizor's hosting provider, Hetzner, had configured its RPKI object to permit` 162.55.0.0/16` with a max length of 24. The adversary launched a hijack for` 162.55.80.0/24` , so it was permitted under Hetzner's RPKI configuration. Hetzner itself was announcing only the /16 variant of the prefix, so the adversary's sub-prefix went uncontested across the vast majority of the Internet. The adversary's route was therefore preferred over Hetzner's` 162.55.0.0/16` when delivering affected packets. Since the adversary could achieve this near-global hijack, MPIC was not able to detect it, and the malicious certificate was issued.


## Not just an edge case, but a trend


At first glance, it seems like we got unlucky due to an edge case. Virtualizor and Hetzner were using RPKI, MPIC was fully deployed, and just one configuration (max length) was set incorrectly. But when you look a bit deeper, there is more to the story. This is not the first time a loose max-length setting enabled a BGP attack and the issuance of a malicious TLS certificate. That is what happened in the[Celer Bridge incident](https://www.coinbase.com/blog/celer-bridge-incident-analysis) , where RPKI was also in use. But the hosting provider was not Hetzner; it was AWS.


So why would a hosting provider as large as AWS misconfigure RPKI? Well, it is a feature, not a bug. Max length exists to give network operators flexibility. Every now and then, Amazon chops up its IP address blocks and gives them to different services and regions based on availability. The allocations are always in flux, so AWS publishes the[current allocations and instructions for receiving change notifications](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/aws-ip-ranges.html#aws-ip-download) . AWS has no central backbone between all its regions. If it were using` 1.2.0.0/16` in a large region but then needed` 1.2.3.0/24` to be carved out and sent to a smaller region, it would begin a new BGP announcement out of the smaller region for` 1.2.3.0/24` .


Max length in its RPKI objects gives AWS the flexibility to do this. The new announcement can be RPKI-valid under the same RPKI object, and this address migration can happen entirely through BGP configurations. For something like this, BGP converges fast (think several seconds or less for most destinations). RPKI information is updated out of band, so avoiding an RPKI update speeds up the process and makes it easier. Does this reintroduce the very sub-prefix attacks RPKI was designed to prevent? **Yes.** But does this technique ensure maximal operational flexibility and the lowest probability of outages while still superficially allowing a provider to respond to FCC pressure and mark its network as “safe” on Cloudflare's Is BGP Safe Yet website? **Also yes.** Humans and businesses constantly seek the path of least resistance; liberal max length is what happens when that philosophy is applied to RPKI.


## So how many people are affected by this problem? A lot


At Crosslayer, we perform complimentary monitoring of 1,000 popular crypto, banking, and high-traffic websites to observe BGP anomalies that might affect the general public. Part of this means breaking these websites down into all their dependencies, including third-party domains serving JavaScript, mapping those out in DNS, and tracking the corresponding DNS server IPs and A-record IPs in BGP.


**Of the 1,000 high-traffic and high-profile websites we monitor, 651 depend on at least one BGP prefix whose max length is set too permissively.** That is roughly twice the number of websites missing RPKI altogether on at least one prefix: 350 websites. Extrapolating from this sample (which is, again, skewed toward top domains) suggests that 65% of all websites could be hit by a BGP attack that exploits max length. This is quite substantial, particularly considering that this window would exist even if base RPKI reached 100% adoption.


## Why this problem is pesky


It seems like the answer is just to make people get max length right, which is somewhat the framing of the[Ars Technica article](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/09/well-executed-bgp-attack-uses-hijacked-ips-to-infect-real-networks/) . But this becomes more difficult once you consider that adopting RPKI largely consists of having network operators write a static rule into a web portal provided by a regional routing registry such as RIPE or ARIN.


Large, dynamic, multiregional networks can experience flux in their BGP-announced prefix lengths. In that environment, getting max length right means deploying a new system to communicate dynamically with the RPKI ecosystem and write new Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) on demand as announcements change. So while adopting RPKI for a cloud provider is largely a configuration concern, configuring max length properly requires engineering a new critical system, one that carries a risk of causing a global outage. I personally suspect this challenge, along with people's desire to be overly liberal, explains why proper max-length adoption is lagging behind RPKI adoption in general.


## What needs to be done


I personally think everyone needs to be doing the type of monitoring we perform at Crosslayer. We do web PKI monitoring and BGP monitoring to detect changes and correlate anomalies between these different systems. This lets us produce a very high-fidelity signal for attacks with very few false positives. Shy of this, simple BGP monitors and Certificate Transparency (CT) monitors work as well. BGP monitoring in isolation is really hard to get right if you do not run your own network, so for many web administrators, good CT monitoring is probably the minimal first step.


I should also note the obvious answer that for people who work with BGP, max length should not be used (unless all covered subprefixes are in the route table). This has[long been the opinion of experts](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/1015) and now even IETF concensus (which is what got max length into the standard in the first place) is[that it should not be used for most cases](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9319/) . While max length use may still persist for the reasons I set forth in this post, it is important operators understand that max length use is generally not recommended.


For those at the application layer, its worth knowning that for better or worse, this problem is concentrated in some providers. There is one that starts with an “A” and ends with a “WS” that has this problem at a massive scale. In fact, Amazon's max-length configurations account for issues in 521 of the 651 websites I previously mentioned as affected. AWS has a massive market share and a notable habit of setting max lengths liberally.


Before anyone from AWS comments that this problem is entirely fixed and all this is old data, review this[AWS prefix in the RIPE RPKI Validator](https://rpki-validator.ripe.net/ui/?prefix=99.84.232.0%2F22&validate-bgp=true) , which serves popular web content and has a max length of /24 with a BGP announcement of /22. AWS even has prefixes with no RPKI, such as[177.71.192.0/20](https://rpki-validator.ripe.net/ui/?prefix=177.71.192.1&asns=AS16509) , which seems to conflict with its[Is BGP Safe Yet](https://isbgpsafeyet.com/) status of “signed + filtering.” AWS not only has this problem; it has been burned by it before. In the[Celer Bridge incident](https://www.coinbase.com/blog/celer-bridge-incident-analysis) , an AWS max-length issue led to the attack.


The anti-AWS is probably Cloudflare, where the majority of max lengths match BGP. For Cloudflare, we most often find discrepancies in prefixes from alternative origins, such as its Magic Transit bring-your-own-IP product. With that said, for pretty much every cloud provider, if you dig deep enough, you can find a discrepancy in some corner of its network. So if you care about this, consider which cloud provider or CDN you use. Crosslayer Labs can evaluate your stack and help confirm that you have made the best choice because we can trace all these problems at scale.


## Conclusion


At first, this looks like a surface vulnerability where a small German provider messed up RPKI and left open an attack vector that should be closed off for high-profile web locations. That is not exactly how I see this situation. One of the largest cloud providers on the Internet today, AWS, has this problem at a massive scale, and so do thousands of other networks and cloud providers. The fix is not just updating one configuration; it is deploying a more intelligent system that can properly sync the out-of-band data of RPKI with the in-band data of BGP announcements. In the meantime, there is nothing to stop this attack from targeting, say,` robinhood.com` (cough, cough,` 3.168.80.0/21` ,[max length 24](https://rpki-validator.ripe.net/ui/?prefix=3.168.80.0%2F21&validate-bgp=true) ).


If there is one takeaway, it is that BGP hijacks against TLS are still a large threat and that max-length issues should be treated with a priority comparable to that of RPKI deployment in general.


---


## For BGP nerds


### In-band versus out-of-band routing security


The RPKI max-length issue is simple on the surface, but it reflects a more nuanced conversation in BGP and routing: in-band versus out-of-band. RPKI is inherently an out-of-band measure. It is a database that lives outside the routing protocol and is then synchronized by systems like the RPKI-to-Router Protocol, which populate filter lists in routers based on this out-of-band data. To avoid the complexity of changing the bytes on the wire of a core routing protocol running between different countries, RPKI keeps the BGP message the same and distributes the security information of interest out of band.


I feel there is little question that information about IP-block ownership can be distributed out of band. It changes rarely, and everyone has a pretty consistent view of a single global state. IP-prefix length is more complex because it challenges both of those assumptions.


### DDoS defense and dynamic prefix lengths


IP-prefix length may need to change rapidly for legitimate reasons. Probably the most notable example is an urgent reroute using a sub-prefix, particularly for DDoS defense. There is a particular type of DDoS defense service that I call “hijack yourself,” which, during a DDoS attack, announces a sub-prefix of the address space being attacked. The idea is that this immediately reroutes traffic to the DDoS defense service, which scrubs the traffic and delivers it.


However, a service like this complicates the ability of networks to set max length correctly. If the network sets max length correctly, the BGP announcement from the DDoS service will be blocked because it is trying to announce a sub-prefix that is not permitted by the max length. Obviously, the DDoS service, in coordination with the original victim network, could push an update to its RPKI object to allow the announcement. But doing so would increase DDoS remediation time from one or two seconds with typical BGP sub-prefix propagation to several minutes or hours based on RPKI data refresh intervals. Those intervals were never intended to be part of a real-time, in-band system.


If the max length is set liberally to permit the DDoS service's announcement, this also permits sub-prefix hijacks. I honestly do not see a long-term way around this, other than moving to CDN-based DDoS services, since the DDoS services are essentially launching a hijack. If we make it so there are no hijacks, you also cannot hijack yourself. BGPSEC could help if it were ever deployed, as path validation could allow the sub-prefix from the DDoS defense service while permitting only announcements signed by that AS's key to propagate.


### Selective announcements for traffic engineering


The other challenge with setting max length is traffic engineering and selective announcement propagation. Backbone-grade BGP is actually a battleground for routing control between networks. In a naïve BGP configuration, the sending network seemingly gets a lot of control over path selection because it holds the packet and picks its favorite route for forwarding that packet. Receiving networks can use several tricks to change this behavior by remotely influencing the sending network's routing-decision algorithm, causing traffic to follow a different path preferred by the receiving network. (One such mechanism is BGP communities, which I studied while writing the[Tango paper](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi24/presentation/birge-lee) , work for which I later won the[Applied Networking Research Prize](https://www.irtf.org/anrp/) .)


The most valuable trick is probably making different announcements with different prefix lengths. Essentially, the receiving network has some preferred neighbors and some less-preferred neighbors. It makes two variations of its IP-prefix announcement: a sub-prefix for the preferred neighbors and a less-specific prefix for its less-preferred neighbors. This is very effective at achieving the network's goal, as any remote network that gets the sub-prefix announcement will always prefer it over the less-specific prefix, steering as much traffic as possible over the links to the preferred neighbors.


Figure 1 shows a topology in which the receiver prefers one route because it uses a cheaper peer link, while the sender prefers a different route because it has fewer hops. While this might sound like a contrived academic BGP example, operators use this approach in the real world to express similar routing preferences.


*Figure 1. The receiver prefers a longer path because it uses a free peering link, whereas the sender prefers a shorter path through a common provider even though it is less preferred by the receiver. In this topology, the receiver can optimize as much traffic as possible over its preferred path by selectively announcing a sub-prefix along the green path, which the sender will universally prefer.*


### Real-world selective-announcement patterns


One example comes from university networks, where many institutions are connected via Internet2, a U.S. academic network with select commercial providers primarily for research computing. Internet2 does not primarily provide broader Internet connectivity, so college students' Netflix connections need a separate commercial provider. However, most institutions strongly prefer to send any eligible traffic over Internet2 because universities typically have significantly more bandwidth on their Internet2 connection than on their commercial connection and expect the network to deliver better performance in general.


This is exactly where selective prefix-length announcements come into play. Giving Internet2 a sub-prefix of the university's global prefix means that any other institution or data center with an Internet2 uplink will prefer the sub-prefix and reach the university over the Internet2 link, regardless of how its local policies are configured.


Another example that an operator described to me involves a hybrid peer/provider relationship with an upstream. The network was big enough and valuable enough to get a peer link with the upstream. In addition, the network also needed to purchase transit and just got a separate provider transit link from the same upstream. The network then announced sub-prefixes over the peer link but a less-specific prefix over the provider link. Any traffic reachable over the peer link traversed it, while the provider link acted as a fallback for traffic from the general Internet.


### Why max-length gaps persist


This is all well and good for traffic engineering (it really works nicely), but it creates a big problem with RPKI: your max length has to match the selectively announced sub-prefix, leaving your global, less-specific prefix vulnerable to global hijacks. Since the sub-prefix is intentionally announced to only part of the Internet, an adversary's malicious announcement would spread uncontested across a large portion of the routing table. I know some cloud providers have experimented with sub-prefix traffic engineering as well, so there is a chance selective sub-prefix announcements are also why we do not see 100% proper max-length configurations across cloud providers.


Because of these issues (DDoS engineering and sub-prefix traffic engineering), discrepancies that permit hijacks may remain even if you have the best system for managing max lengths.
